summaries.title: ADP National Employment Report February 2026
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from ADP reveals that private sector employment increased by 63,000 jobs in February 2026, with annual pay rising 4.5% year-over-year. The report, produced in collaboration with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, analyzes anonymized weekly payroll data from over 26 million private-sector employees in the U.S. Dr. Nela Richardson, ADP's chief economist, noted, “We've seen an increase in hiring and pay gains remain solid, especially for job-stayers,” though hiring was concentrated in a few sectors, leading to a record low pay premium for changing jobs.

In detail, the report highlights:

**Jobs Report:**
- Private employers added 63,000 jobs in February, marking the best job gains since July 2025.
- Growth was particularly strong in the construction and education/health services sectors.
- Breakdown by industry:
  - Goods-producing added 16,000 jobs.
  - Service-providing added 47,000 jobs, with notable contributions from education/health services (58,000 jobs) and information (11,000 jobs).
- Regional changes indicated the South gained the most jobs (37,000), while the Midwest lost 4,000.
- Job creation varied by establishment size, with small establishments adding 60,000 jobs.

**Pay Insights:**
- Pay for job-stayers increased by 4.5% year-over-year, remaining stable from the previous month.
- For job-changers, annualized pay growth slowed to 6.3%.
- Pay growth varied by industry and firm size, with small firms showing the lowest growth rates.

The report also revised January's employment figures, lowering the number of jobs added from 22,000 to 11,000. The next ADP National Employment Report is scheduled for release on April 1, 2026.

Source URL: https://adp-ri-nrip-static.adp.com/artifacts/us_ner/20260304/ADP_NATIONAL_EMPLOYMENT_REPORT_Press_Release_2026_02%20FINAL.pdf

As hiring focuses on sectors like construction and education, the employment landscape showcases both opportunities and challenges ahead.

summaries.title: How Will the Iran Conflict Impact Oil Prices?
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Goldman Sachs details the impacts of escalating conflicts in Iran on oil prices. Following US and Israeli military actions, oil prices surged, influenced significantly by potential transit disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies.

Goldman Sachs strategists indicate a risk premium of about $14 per barrel, reflecting increased trader demands following the conflict. The report outlines estimates suggesting that a full month of blocked flows could lead to price increases of $15 per barrel without offsets, with various scenarios providing lower estimates depending on the utilization of spare pipeline capacities and strategic reserve releases.

Historical patterns indicate temporary spikes in oil prices can follow geopolitical events; for example, during mid-2022, oil prices exceeded estimated fair value to a significant extent due to similar uncertainties. In 2025, Iran produced approximately 3.5 million barrels per day (mb/d) of crude, contributing about 4% to global supplies, and faced ongoing export levels of 1.7 mb/d for crude and condensates.

The report warns that LNG prices could significantly rise if transit through the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, with estimates suggesting European gas prices might reach approximately 74 EUR/MWh if LNG flows are fully halted for a month, and over 100 EUR/MWh in cases of longer disruptions. 

This article serves an educational purpose, and Goldman Sachs disclaims any obligations regarding its accuracy or liability. 

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/how-will-the-iran-conflict-impact-oil-prices

summaries.title: Why Has Productivity in the US Construction Industry Stagnated?
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Goldman Sachs examines the stagnation of productivity in the US construction industry, noting that this trend has been pronounced since 1965, with an average decline of 0.6% per year compared to a 1.6% growth in the wider economy. Economist Elsie Peng attributes several factors to the underperformance, including a lack of innovation, increasing housing regulation, and measurement issues.

The report highlights that technological advancements in the construction sector have been limited, with major machinery largely unchanged since the 1950s and pre-fabrication technology usage declining from contributing one-third of new housing units in the 1960s to just 5% today. Additionally, the construction sector has not capitalized on innovations from other industries, resulting in a lower boost to productivity than seen in sectors such as pharmaceuticals.

Housing regulation has also negatively impacted productivity, with Goldman Sachs Research indicating that a 1% increase in regulation can lead to a 0.6 percentage point drop in annual productivity growth. Specifically, strict land use regulations and approval delays contribute significantly to this decline, worsening the housing crisis in the US.

Finally, the report suggests that mismeasurements in construction output may be biasing productivity data. By not accounting for quality improvements in housing and using flawed price indices for deflating nonresidential structures, actual productivity growth may be worse than reported.

Source URL: https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/why-has-productivity-in-the-us-construction-industry-stagnated

Economist Elsie Peng attributes this lack of growth to factors including outdated technology, increasing housing regulations, and potential mismeasurements in output, painting a stark picture of an industry struggling to innovate while the economy evolves around it.

summaries.title: Dodge Momentum Index Declines 7% in February
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Dodge Construction Network reveals that the Dodge Momentum Index (DMI) declined by 7.3% in February, reaching 250.0, down from a downwardly revised January figure of 269.8. Commercial planning saw an 8.9% drop, while institutional planning slowed by 4.0%. According to Sarah Martin, Associate Director of Forecasting at Dodge Construction Network, “Planning momentum continued to normalize in February after a surge in activity in the back half of 2025.” 

The report notes that risks related to costs, labor, and geopolitics are likely to hinder builder confidence in the short term, although a robust planning pipeline points to potential construction spending acceleration in 2027. In the commercial sector, planning momentum decreased across all sectors except for warehouses. All institutional sectors also experienced slowdowns, with public buildings facing significant contraction. Nevertheless, areas such as retail stores, recreational buildings, data centers, and healthcare facilities displayed elevated project momentum.

Compared to February 2025, the DMI increased by 18.7%. The commercial segment rose by 12.3% (4.4% growth excluding data centers), and the institutional segment surged by 34.0% year-over-year. In February, 23 projects valued at $100 million or more commenced planning, including notable commercial projects like the $500 million CyrusOne Data Center in Whitney, Texas, and the $448 million TX12 Data Center in San Antonio, Texas. Major institutional projects included the $400 million Orange County Convention Center Grand Concourse expansion in Orlando, Florida, and a $254 million school replacement project in Upper Marlboro, Maryland. 

The DMI serves as a monthly indicator based on a three-month moving value of nonresidential building projects in planning, which typically leads nonresidential construction spending by approximately one to 18 months. 

Source URL: https://www.construction.com/dodge-momentum-index/dodge-momentum-index-declines-7-in-february/
summaries.headline: Dodge Momentum Index Plummets 7.3% in February Amid Cost and Labor Concerns
summaries.blurb: The Dodge Momentum Index (DMI) experienced a significant 7.3% decline in February, highlighting ongoing concerns in both cost and labor that are impacting builder confidence. Despite this dip, the long-term outlook remains promising, with a robust planning pipeline indicating a potential acceleration in construction spending by 2027. Notable commercial projects, including two massive data centers in Texas and a major convention center expansion in Florida, illustrate pockets of growth amid the slowdown.

summaries.title: Construction Starts Grow 1% in January
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from Dodge Construction Network highlights that total construction starts increased by 0.7% in January 2026 to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $1.24 trillion. Nonresidential building starts declined by 15.4%, residential starts fell by 6.4%, while nonbuilding starts surged by 24.3%. Year-over-year, total construction starts rose by 5.0%, despite nonresidential starts down by 10.3% and residential starts down by 17.0%. 

In the residential sector, construction starts fell to an annual rate of $345 billion, with single-family starts increasing by 1.5% month-over-month, while multifamily starts decreased by 17.8%. Compared to January 2025, residential starts were down 17.0%. The largest multifamily projects started include the $335 million 38 Gramercy Park East Condominiums in New York.

For nonresidential building, construction starts dropped to $378 billion. While commercial starts plummeted by 27.3%, certain areas like warehouses and retail saw increases. It was noted that the manufacturing sector experienced significant growth, up by 97.5% in January. 

In the nonbuilding category, the $522 billion rate was heavily influenced by a dramatic increase of 184.8% in electric power/utilities. Key projects included the $12 billion Port Arthur LNG project in Texas.

Regionally, construction starts increased in the Northeast, South Central, and South Atlantic, while they declined in the West and Midwest. 

Source URL: https://www.construction.com/company-news/construction-starts-grow-1-in-january-2/
summaries.headline: Construction Starts Up 0.7% in January Amid Mixed Sector Performance
summaries.blurb: In January 2026, total construction starts saw a modest increase of 0.7%, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $1.24 trillion, according to the latest report from Dodge Construction Network. While nonresidential and residential sectors faced declines, a remarkable surge in nonbuilding projects—particularly a staggering 184.8% rise in electric power and utilities—signals shifting dynamics in the industry. Key projects, including the $12 billion Port Arthur LNG facility, highlight the sector's resilience amidst mixed performance.

summaries.title: Industrial MSA Deep Dive: Near-Full Occupancy & Minimal CMBS Delinquency
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Trepp discusses the robust performance of the industrial real estate sector in the United States, highlighting minimal delinquency rates and high occupancy levels as of February 2026. 

Occupancy rates for industrial properties in the top 25 metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) are notably strong, with Charlotte, Pittsburgh, and St. Louis reporting 100% occupancy. Other significant markets such as Riverside-San Bernardino, Phoenix, New York, and San Francisco maintain occupancy rates between approximately 98.5% and 99.8%, resulting in an average occupancy rate above 92% across these MSAs.

Delinquency rates for industrial loans are exceptionally low, with a weighted average of just 0.37%. The highest delinquency in the top 25 MSAs is seen in Chicago at 2.45%, while other notable rates include Boston at 1.73% and Tampa at 1.24%. Many metropolitan areas report nearly zero delinquent industrial loans, indicating strong loan performance in this sector compared to multifamily delinquency rates, which are closer to 50-60 basis points.

Capital markets activity reflects these positive fundamentals, with approximately $3.8 billion in industrial loan originations in the fourth quarter of 2025. Riverside-San Bernardino led the origination activity, followed by Atlanta, New York, Los Angeles, and Dallas-Fort Worth. The transactions are characterized by significant portfolio deals usually driven by institutional investors seeking operational efficiencies.

The overall conclusion is that the industrial real estate sector remains one of the most stable within the commercial real estate market, demonstrating solid occupancy, minimal delinquency, and continued capital inflow.

Source URL: https://www.trepp.com/trepptalk/industrial-msa-deep-dive

summaries.title: Construction Employment Falls By 11,000 In February With Declines In Residential And Nonresidential As Firms Worry About Demand Levels
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from the Associated General Contractors of America reveals that construction employment fell by 11,000 jobs in February, encompassing both residential and nonresidential sectors. This decline comes on the heels of stronger hiring in January, which had been reported more favorably than initially understood. The current downturn indicates that contractors are adopting a more cautious stance regarding workforce expansion, primarily due to uncertainties related to material prices and project demand.

Macrina Wilkins, the association’s director of market insights, stated, “Contractors may be more reluctant to add workers amid uncertainty about how much they will pay for construction materials and demand for certain types of construction projects.” Despite this monthly drop, the construction employment sector has experienced growth at a faster pace compared to the broader economy over the past year, underscoring the sector's resilience even in the face of current challenges.

The report emphasizes that both residential and nonresidential construction areas have seen job losses, reflecting a broader trend of caution among firms as they reassess their hiring strategies in light of prevailing economic conditions. The overall employment picture within the construction industry remains a point of discussion as firms grapple with these evolving challenges.

Source URL: https://news.agc.org/economics/construction-employment-falls-by-11000-in-february-with-declines-in-residential-and-nonresidential-as-firms-worry-about-demand-levels/

This cautious trend, following a surge in hiring the previous month, highlights contractors' growing concerns about fluctuating material costs and demand for projects. Despite this setback, the construction industry continues to outpace the broader economy in job growth over the past year, showcasing its resilience amid uncertainty.

summaries.title: Extreme Increases In Aluminum, Steel And Copper Costs Drive Up Prices For Construction Materials In January; Spending Ends 2025 Down From 2024
summaries.summaryText:
A February report from AGC Construction Data highlights significant cost increases in construction materials, with the producer price index for materials and services used in nonresidential construction rising by 2.9 percent from January 2025 to February 2026. The report also notes a decline in construction spending, which fell by 0.4 percent from December 2024 to December 2025. This analysis was conducted by the Associated General Contractors of America based on two government reports released on the same date.

The association's officials attribute the rising costs to tariffs on key materials, which they argue inflate prices. They are calling on federal officials to promptly renew vital infrastructure legislation, such as the surface transportation bill, to provide stability for domestic suppliers, which in turn may lead to increased production.

Ken Simonson, the association’s chief economist, stated, “Although producer indexes are based on selling prices of domestic producers, the steep tariffs on imported metals and products are clearly enabling U.S. sellers to push up costs for construction materials and equipment.” Simonson emphasized that ensuring domestic producers have greater certainty regarding future demand could incentivize them to enhance production capacities, potentially resulting in lower prices for construction materials in the long term.

Overall, the findings underline economic pressures within the construction sector, particularly regarding material costs and spending trends, while also highlighting the influence of policy decisions on production and pricing.

Source URL: https://news.agc.org/economics/extreme-increases-in-aluminum-steel-and-copper-costs-drive-up-prices-for-construction-materials-in-january-spending-ends-2025-down-from-2024/

summaries.blurb: A new report from AGC Construction Data reveals a concerning 2.9 percent spike in construction material costs, driven largely by tariffs on essential metals like aluminum, steel, and copper. While construction spending has dipped slightly, industry leaders stress the urgency for renewed infrastructure legislation to stabilize prices and boost domestic production. This dynamic landscape underscores the critical link between policy decisions and economic pressures facing the construction sector.

summaries.title: An Updated Outlook for the U.S. Economy
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from J.P. Morgan Asset Management provides an updated outlook for the U.S. economy, revisiting forecasts made three weeks prior in light of recent economic data and significant geopolitical events. 

The earlier forecast anticipated a real GDP growth of 2% year-over-year by the fourth quarter of 2026, with specific projections for quarterly growth, job trends, earnings, and inflation rates. It expected real GDP growth of just 1% in the first quarter and a recovering pace of 3% in subsequent quarters, although slowing to 1% later in the year. Jobs were projected to see minimal payroll gains, with a decline in the workforce due to shifting demographics, leading to an unemployment rate of around 4.0% by the end of 2026. Profit growth for S&P 500 companies was forecasted at double digits, while CPI inflation was predicted to peak at over 3% during the summer before settling near 2% by year-end.

Recent developments impacting the economic outlook include a lower-than-expected real GDP growth of 1.4% in the previous quarter, weak job reports showing significant payroll losses, and ongoing geopolitical tensions following the start of a war in the Middle East. The Supreme Court's recent decision to strike down IEEPA tariffs prompted a swift response from the Administration, reinstating tariffs at a new high of 10% with expected increases.

From these new insights, the revised outlook anticipates lower consumer and business confidence due to war and rising gasoline prices, leading to a decline in spending, albeit partially offset by increased government and energy infrastructure investment. The fourth quarter growth forecast now sits at 1.8%. Unemployment may reduce marginally to 4.2% by December 2026 despite a recent rise in the unemployment rate.

Profit expectations have been adjusted to high single-digit growth due to ongoing productivity boosts and AI spending, while CPI inflation might peak at 3.5% in June before tapering to around 1.9% by year-end. The Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates steady in March and potentially implement two rate cuts throughout 2026 in light of the evolving economic landscape.

The report underscores the increased market uncertainty and suggests diversified investment strategies as vital for navigating the current geopolitical and economic volatility. 

Source URL: https://am.jpmorgan.com/us/en/asset-management/adv/insights/market-insights/market-updates/notes-on-the-week-ahead/an-updated-outlook-for-the-us-economy/

summaries.title: Does war in Iran change the 2026 outlook?
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from J.P. Morgan Asset Management discusses the potential impact of conflict in Iran on the 2026 economic outlook. The report outlines how financial markets typically respond to geopolitical events with initial volatility, especially in risk assets and oil prices, while safe havens gain traction. These moves are usually temporary as U.S. investors recognize that most geopolitical tensions are localized and have limited direct effects on domestic growth.

However, the situation in Iran poses risks, particularly due to its influence on energy markets. Although Iran's oil production has diminished due to sanctions, it accounts for approximately 5% of global oil supply and has the capacity to disrupt key energy infrastructure, especially through the Strait of Hormuz, which facilitates about one-fifth of the world's oil transit. Insurers have begun withdrawing "war-risk" coverage, complicating shipping routes, while regional attacks on oil facilities further threaten supply.

Nevertheless, several factors could mitigate the impact of these disruptions. The U.S. government has indicated readiness to support shipping insurance and enhance naval protection for oil tankers. Furthermore, the global energy market in 2026 remains robust, with OPEC+ maintaining spare capacity, U.S. shale production at historic levels, and low demand for heating as warmer months approach.

The U.S. economy's diminished dependence on oil, as evidenced by reduced energy consumption per GDP unit, along with its status as a net energy exporter, lessens its vulnerability to energy price surges. Although energy price spikes could occur, they are more likely to lead to inflation rather than an economic recession.

The report advises investors that the muted market reactions highlight the transient nature of geopolitical risk premiums. Maintaining diversification across asset classes and regions is recommended as a prudent strategy amid potential market shocks. 

Source URL: https://am.jpmorgan.com/us/en/asset-management/adv/insights/market-insights/market-updates/on-the-minds-of-investors/does-war-in-iran-change-the-2026-outlook/

summaries.title: 6 Reasons Why Today’s Construction Labor Environment Will Likely Increase Disputes & Litigation In 2026
summaries.summaryText:
A found article from The Providence Journal dated 2026-03-17 titled "6 Reasons Why Today’s Construction Labor Environment Will Likely Increase Disputes & Litigation In 2026" reports the following:

Fundamental changes in the U.S. construction labor market have occurred affecting costs, availability, capabilities and timeliness.
For the long-term health of the construction industry, labor issues must become a top priority, to be able to deliver the quality & consistency expected, ultimately, reducing the number of disputes.” — James F. Gallagher, P.E., F.ASCE, Principal – RMC
MARLTON, NJ, UNITED STATES, March 17, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — In 2026, the U.S. commercial construction industry is expected to grow at a rate of only about 2%, continuing 2025’s lackluster industry performance. Although commercial construction growth will be marginal, the number of construction disputes and litigation is expected to rise in 2026, according to James Gallagher, P.E., F.ASCE and CEO of Resolution Management Consultants.
“Over the last few years, fundamental changes in the U.S. construction labor market have occurred affecting costs, availability and capabilities. These changes are having a significant impact on construction companies achieving contract compliance, triggering a higher incidence of disputes and litigation,” said Gallagher. Gallagher observes that these changes aren’t completely new, however due to the relative slowness in volume, over the last few years, the full effects of labor’s influence haven’t fully affected the industry. He believes that both new projects and the completion of existing projects will start to feel labor’s effects this year, with the potential to trigger a higher number of disputes in 2026 than in the past.
Gallagher, who is a construction management and dispute resolution thought leader, identifies 6 factors, in particular, that are causing labor’s elevated influence on construction disputes and litigation. They include:
1) The Federal government’s focus on illegal immigration enforcement.
Let’s face it – the construction industry employs and has employed a number of illegal immigrants. Whatever you think about that phenomenon; over the last year, the U.S. Government has changed its priority to focus on immigration enforcement, resulting in the construction industry losing some of its labor force. As the labor force shrinks, it will take longer to complete projects, causing timing and quality disputes.
2) Due to the law of supply and demand, labor prices likely will rise.
As the construction labor force continues to shrink while demand is growing, the effect will be that overall labor costs will rise. Rising costs will cause construction contractors to miss contracted time and budget targets, triggering disputes and litigation.
3) Cutting back on apprenticeship programs has limited the number of skilled young people entering the construction industry.
The number of apprenticeship programs available have been reduced 2-5% each year over the last few years. These cutbacks will result in fewer skilled workers in the industry affecting contract fulfillment and quality.
4) Reduced quality due to lowered labor skill/qualification standards.
In order to include more people in the construction labor force, standards have been reduced in a number of areas, including depth of training, experience and qualification. The reduction in standards is causing a reduction in quality in many areas, leading to an increase in disputes.
5) The construction workforce is aging (and retiring).
At the other end of the spectrum, the aging and retiring of older construction workers will be shrinking the available workforce causing slowdowns and quality limitations in completing projects as contracted, leading to more disputes.
6) Limited training for new, labor-saving technologies will mean slower implementation.
There is a serious lack of training programs available to construction workers, especially those that train advanced, labor-saving technologies, such as drones, BIM, AI, data analytics and more. The limited availability of proper training reduce their introduction and widespread use ultimately keeping costs higher than expected, potentially leading to disputes.
One positive note: Gallagher predicts that because the cost of litigation has risen significantly in recent years, more disputes will be settled outside of the courtroom in 2026 where they will be settled more quickly and less expensively. He said, “For the long-term health of the construction industry, labor issues must become a top priority, in order to be able to deliver the quality and consistency expected and ultimately, to reduce the number of disputes.”

Source URL: https://www.providencejournal.com/press-release/story/44655/6-reasons-why-todays-construction-labor-environment-will-likely-increase-disputes-litigation-in-2026/

summaries.title: Special Servicing Rate Falls in February, Led by Office & Mixed-Use, Despite Retail Surge
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Trepp highlights the trends in the CMBS Special Servicing Rate for February, showing a modest decline of 18 basis points to 10.73%. This decrease was primarily due to seven office and three mixed-use loans transferring out of special servicing; however, this was almost counterbalanced by a substantial retail loan that moved into special servicing.

The report notes varying movements across different property types. The mixed-use rate decreased significantly by 118 basis points to 12.49%, and the office rate fell by 82 basis points to 16.29%. In contrast, the industrial sector remained stable, with no change at 0.85%. The retail segment experienced an increase of 133 basis points, rising to 13.09%, primarily driven by one loan contributing 120 basis points to this increase. Additionally, the lodging rate saw a rise of 64 basis points, reaching 10.01%, while multifamily properties experienced a smaller uptick of 16 basis points, now at 8.30%.

During February, new transfers into special servicing amounted to $2.66 billion across 50 loans. The document suggests that detailed information about the specific loans influencing these rate movements can be accessed through a download link provided in the report.

For individuals seeking further insights into the mechanics of special servicing rates, Trepp offers "Special Servicing 101: Trepp's Essential Guide to the Management & Resolution of Distressed CMBS Loans." 

The data presented is based on information that is widely available to the public and believed to be accurate.

summaries.title: CRE CLO Issuance Surges to Start 2026, Putting 2021 Peak Levels Within Reach
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Trepp details a significant surge in commercial real estate collateralized loan obligation (CRE CLO) issuance at the start of 2026, positioning the market for a strong year reminiscent of 2021 peak levels. As of early March, total CRE CLO issuance reached $11.2 billion, marking a 34% increase compared to $8.3 billion during the same period in 2025.

This robust first-quarter activity suggests that issuance could range from $30 billion to $40 billion for the entirety of 2026, with a possibility of reaching $45 billion if the current pace continues. In contrast to 2021's record volumes, largely driven by low interest rates, today's issuance occurs in a higher-rate environment, reflecting a more nuanced lending activity involving transitional or value-add loans. Some critics note instances of “bridge-to-bridge” lending, but many of these transactions are linked to operational improvements rather than mere rate fluctuations.

The multifamily sector remains dominant, comprising approximately 70% of CRE CLO collateral in 2025, a trend that has persisted into 2026. Meanwhile, office exposure has sharply declined, dropping from 14% in 2021 to about 1.2% in 2025. Current collateral composition includes 69.6% multifamily, 11.2% industrial, 4.0% lodging, 2.8% office, 2.1% retail, and 10.3% other sectors.

Underwriting expectations have shifted since 2021, with today’s projections indicating more conservative, single-digit rent growth assumptions, contributing to a more stable loan performance outlook. The early 2026 CRE CLO activity has emerged as a promising development in commercial real estate finance, signifying its potential as a primary financing avenue for transitional and value-add strategies.

Source URL: https://www.trepp.com/trepptalk/cre-clo-issuance-start-2026

summaries.title: The Leadership Gap in Construction: What Companies Can’t Afford to Ignore
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from FMI Corp discusses the leadership gap in the construction industry and the challenges that arise as companies experience growth without proportionate leadership capacity. Despite increased revenues and headcounts, many organizations struggle to keep pace with the complexity of their operations, leading to a widening gap between the capabilities of their leaders and the demands of their roles.

Matt Kennedy, a partner at FMI Corp, describes this issue as a mathematical problem rather than one of culture or talent pipeline. He notes, “Businesses are growing faster than the people leading them,” indicating that many firms are not adequately prepared for their scale. Senior leaders recognize the issue but often lack the time to address it, as they are preoccupied with tight project margins and ongoing demands.

This gap manifests gradually, resulting in delayed decision-making, increased reliance on senior leaders for routine matters, and diminished project performance. Tracey Smith, also a partner at FMI Corp, highlights that increasing project speeds and complexities require different leadership responsibilities than in the past. Failure to adapt can hinder strategic management and elevate operational risks.

The report identifies the retirement of experienced project managers as a growing concern, with fewer qualified successors ready to fill these roles. Kennedy and Smith emphasize that construction firms often resort to reactive measures to manage immediate pressures, which hampers effective succession planning and leads to overburdened senior executives.

To address these issues, the report outlines five recommendations for developing leadership depth:

1. Evaluate your leadership bench: Assess performance at all levels and define what effective leadership means for each layer of the organization.
   
2. Prioritize key leadership capabilities: Focus on one or two essential skills and consistently reinforce and measure them before expanding.
   
3. Integrate succession planning into operations: Identify potential successors early and provide them with opportunities to prepare through challenging roles.
   
4. Redefine leadership roles upon promotion: Offer coaching to help emerging leaders transition from technical tasks to broader responsibilities.
   
5. Encourage regular feedback: Establish clear expectations and provide ongoing performance feedback to help emerging leaders understand their progress and how to advance.

Kennedy encourages firms to conduct a “bench reality check” to honestly assess their current leadership against defined standards of effectiveness. This evaluation can help identify areas where execution risks are likely to emerge and inform strategies to bolster leadership capacity.

A March 30, 2026, report from Clark Hill discusses the U.S. Department of Labor's (DOL) proposed rule to increase prevailing wage levels for immigration sponsorship, published on March 27, 2026. This proposed rule aims to significantly raise wage requirements for sponsorship programs, impacting H-1B professionals and many employment-based immigrant workers, aligning with the Administration's immigration policy to protect U.S. workers. 

The rule proposes to improve wage calculations by ensuring that prevailing wages reflect what U.S. workers are paid for similar jobs, thus reducing the incentive for employers to replace U.S. workers with lower-paid foreign nationals. Employers must offer at least the prevailing wage as determined by the DOL, with levels classified from Entry Level to Fully Competent, based on skills and experience. The DOL argues that the current wage levels, set in 2005, are outdated, creating a significant discrepancy—over $19,000 on average—between what U.S. workers earn and what is available to foreign applicants.

The new calculation system would shift existing prevailing wage levels towards higher percentiles, effective immediately, particularly affecting entry-level sponsorships by potentially eliminating Level I (17th percentile) wages. This change could create recruitment challenges for small employers and startups in high-demand sectors like technology and engineering due to increased hiring costs for foreign talent. 

The proposed rule maintains the allowance for employers to use other wage surveys for compliance but will increase scrutiny on such practices. It also introduces updated regulations for Labor Condition Applications when employers discover they are not paying the determined prevailing wage, providing a 30-day window to address discrepancies without regulatory violations.

Written comments on the proposed rule can be submitted until May 26, 2026. If adopted, the changes would take effect 30 to 60 days post-publication and apply to all pending requests as well as future Labor Condition Applications. The timing may coincide with the FY27 H-1B Cap petitions, which began a new weighted-wage lottery.

summaries.title: The Outlook for Private Credit amid Rising Market Stress
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Goldman Sachs discusses the state of private credit markets amid rising investor concerns over unrecognized risks. Vivek Bantwal, global co-head of private credit in Goldman Sachs Asset Management, emphasizes that fundamentals in private credit appear strong, despite some investors withdrawing funds due to risk apprehensions. 

Data reveals that defaults and overdue loans remain low, with many managers providing reassuring disclosures of double-digit growth in revenue and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA). Bantwal notes that the withdrawal of some retail investors may lead to higher yields in the private credit market, particularly as this sector has seen rapid growth by attracting affluent individual investors, often through business development companies (BDCs) and evergreen structures. However, an oversimplified understanding of these "semi-liquid" funds may contribute to investor hesitation.

Bantwal expresses caution about potential risks, citing the absence of a true credit cycle since the recovery from the Global Financial Crisis and the presence of new, untested players in private credit. While performance in both public and private credit markets remains strong, he highlights that underwriting standards may weaken during long periods of stability, indicating a future risk during economic downturns.

Concerns also exist regarding exposure to software and technology companies, particularly in light of AI disruption. Many private credit managers have a substantial portion of their portfolios in this sector, but Bantwal reassures that lending typically occurs at the top of the capital structure, ensuring some protection against losses. The performance of private credit portfolios may diverge significantly, influenced by the resilience of individual companies within the software domain.

summaries.title: Labor force growth, breakeven employment, and potential GDP growth
summaries.summaryText:
A report from the Federal Reserve published on April 2, 2026, discusses trends in labor force growth, breakeven employment, and potential GDP growth. The authors, Seth Murray and Ivan Vidangos, indicate that labor force growth in the U.S. has significantly slowed and could approach near-zero levels due to factors such as low population growth from decreased immigration and declining labor force participation associated with an aging population. This trend is described as unprecedented in recent U.S. history.

The article outlines two main implications of this slowdown: first, that breakeven employment growth, or the number of jobs required to keep the unemployment rate steady, would also be near-zero. This situation makes the likelihood of negative job growth nearly equal to positive job growth in any given month. Second, any potential GDP growth will have to come exclusively from productivity growth, as labor force growth is anticipated to be insufficient.

The potential labor force is defined as the population aged 16 and older who are either employed or actively seeking employment. Historical data shows that, on average, labor force growth has been about 1.4 percent annually since 1960, largely driven by population growth, which has averaged 1.3 percent annually. However, projections for 2026 predict the weakest population growth since 1951, contributing to a potential labor force growth rate that could drop below 0.2 percent.

With the projected drop in population growth exacerbated by a declining potential labor force participation rate, it is expected that the available workforce could increase by less than 10,000 workers per month in 2026. This would mark a significant economic change, with a breakeven growth pace for jobs expected to require fewer than 10,000 new jobs monthly, contrasting sharply with historical averages. Such low estimates point toward a potential reality where job growth in any month could be negative, despite economic output potentially growing at a rate similar to potential output growth.

The authors also discuss historical patterns of potential GDP growth, delineating how it has typically been supported by both potential employment increases and productivity enhancements. The shifts noted in the 2026 estimates project nearly zero potential employment growth, indicating any further GDP growth will rely heavily on rising productivity.

In conclusion, the report stresses that the slowing labor force growth isn't just a temporary issue but may be a lasting trend, likely influenced by ongoing demographic factors and immigration patterns. The profound changes highlighted in this note illustrate a critical transition in U.S. labor market dynamics and economic growth characteristics.

Source URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/labor-force-growth-breakeven-employment-and-potential-gdp-growth-20260402.html

summaries.title: Construction Delivery Methods: A Legal Perspective
summaries.summaryText:
A March report from Clark Hill outlines various construction project delivery methods and their legal implications. The article discusses four primary methods: Design-Bid-Build, Design-Build, Construction Manager Advisor (CMA), and Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR).

**Design-Bid-Build** is the most traditional method where the project owner holds two separate contracts—one with an architect/engineer for the project design and another with a contractor for construction. This method ensures objective selection of the lowest bidder and includes three distinct phases: design, bidding, and construction. However, the separation of responsibilities can lead to a lack of collaboration, negatively impacting the budget and schedule.

**Design-Build** differs by allowing the contractor to handle both design and construction under one contract, which can lead to better communication and fewer disputes. This method is advantageous for addressing design challenges early and potentially lowering costs and project duration. However, it also carries risks of corner-cutting due to reliance on preliminary designs and the commitment to a lump sum or guaranteed maximum price.

**Construction Manager Advisor (CMA)** and **Construction Management at Risk (CMAR)** are management-based methods where the owner retains a construction manager for preconstruction services. In CMA, the manager acts as an advisor without contracting directly with subcontractors. In contrast, CMAR allows the construction manager to contract directly with subcontractors, assuming risk for costs and timelines. A guaranteed maximum price may be established, though it's not universally applicable.

The article emphasizes the importance of selecting the appropriate method and advocating for consultation with a construction attorney to tailor contracts accordingly.

The filing process involves two sets of validations—file declaration validations and entry-specific validations—ensuring that submissions meet required formats and that only applicable entries are processed. Should any errors occur, they can be corrected, and entries can be resubmitted.

Importers are urged to begin compiling necessary data now, confirming their ACH refund enrollment, and segregating entries into different categories based on their eligibility for refunds. CBP will also provide a Quick Reference Guide for CAPE users on its website.

summaries.title: FOMC Minutes - March 2026 Meeting
summaries.summaryText:
A report from the Federal Reserve, published on April 8, 2026, outlines the minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee's March 2026 meeting.

The meeting commenced on March 17 and continued the following day, during which financial market developments were reviewed. Concerns regarding disruptions from artificial intelligence (AI) initially lowered policy rate expectations, but a subsequent conflict in the Middle East caused a spike in energy prices, impacting macroeconomic outlooks. Oil prices surged by approximately 50%, although longer-term expectations remained relatively stable. Financial market responses included a higher implied path for the federal funds rate, reflecting anticipated rate hikes.

Equity prices dipped, particularly in the software sector, attributed to AI disruptions. In contrast, foreign equities outperformed U.S. equities early in 2026 but faced declines amid the conflict. Money market conditions remained stable, with the federal funds rate unchanged. The Committee also anticipated growth in the System Open Market Account holdings, particularly due to expected reserve management purchases in light of tax payments affecting treasury accounts.

Economic indicators showed steady GDP growth, although the unemployment rate remained largely unchanged. Inflation, measured by the personal consumption expenditures index, showed slight increases, with consumer price inflation at 2.8% in January and core inflation at 3.1%. Job creation remained sluggish, impacted by a healthcare sector strike and extreme weather. Projections indicated a continuation of GDP growth in line with potential growth rates through 2028.

Participants expressed varied outlooks on inflation, recognizing persistent above-target levels and possible risks from geopolitical tensions, particularly related to oil prices. Concerns about labor market conditions were raised, noting low job growth and potential vulnerabilities from AI developments.

Concerning monetary policy, most participants agreed to maintain the federal funds rate range at 3.5% to 3.75%, highlighting uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook and geopolitical developments. A minority suggested a decrease in the target range due to risks of weak labor demand.

The meeting concluded with a commitment to monitor incoming data and adjust policy as necessary based on evolving economic dynamics and risks to inflation and employment. The next meeting was scheduled for April 28-29, 2026.

summaries.title: Look Before You Leap: Legal Considerations For Contractors Pursuing Work In A New State
summaries.summaryText:
A April report from Clark Hill discusses the legal considerations contractors must address when pursuing work in a new state. Contractors often seek new opportunities due to changing market trends, but they must first understand the state's laws regarding licensing, prompt payment, lien claims, risk-shifting contract clauses, and labor laws.

**State Licensing Requirements:** Contractors need to determine if a state contractor’s license is necessary, as requirements can vary widely across states. Some states require licensure at both state and local levels, and there may be specific regulations based on trade classifications. Working without a license can result in severe penalties, including financial repercussions and legal charges.

**Prompt Pay Statutes:** Different states have varying prompt pay statutes that govern payment timing and obligations between owners and contractors. Understanding these laws can help contractors avoid penalties for delayed payments and leverage rights in case of slow-paying owners.

**Lien Laws/Waiver Forms:** Liens are crucial for enforcing payment on private projects. Each state's lien laws are unique and can be complex, impacting a contractor's ability to secure payment. Different states have diverse requirements for filing liens, making it essential for contractors to familiarize themselves with these rules before commencing work.

**Variations in Risk-Shifting Contract Clauses:** Common contractual clauses concerning indemnification and payment can have different enforceability across states. States may have specific statutes that limit or void particular indemnity provisions, and certain "magic language" may be required for pay-if-paid clauses to be valid.

**State Labor and Safety Laws:** Contractors should be aware of state-specific labor laws, especially regarding union presence and project labor agreements. Safety regulations can also vary significantly, with some states enforcing stricter standards than federal guidelines, necessitating compliance by contractors.

Overall, while expanding operations into new states offers opportunities, contractors should approach this endeavor carefully, ensuring compliance with local laws and regulations. Many resources, including state websites and trade organizations, are available to assist in navigating these complexities.

summaries.title: Tracking Trillions: The Assumptions Shaping the Scale of the AI Build-Out
summaries.summaryText:
A May 2026 report from Goldman Sachs titled "Tracking Trillions: The Assumptions Shaping the Scale of the AI Build-Out" delves into the complexities surrounding the capital expenditure (CapEx) required for AI infrastructure. 

The analysis emphasizes that the estimated investment in AI infrastructure, projected between $4 trillion to $8 trillion over the next five years, is highly conditional, reliant on a small number of assumptions about the infrastructure's development and renewal. Key factors that influence these estimates include the economic lifespan of AI chips, the costs and complexities involved in constructing next-generation data centers, chip architectural choices, and potential physical or institutional bottlenecks that could delay the build-out.

The report provides baseline estimates of nearly $7.6 trillion in capital investment between 2026 and 2031, anchored by projected revenue from NVIDIA's data center sales. The expenditure is primarily allocated toward AI accelerators, data centers, and associated power systems. For example, the document notes that AI accelerators typically have a useful life span of four to six years, which plays a significant role in determining overall capital needs, as shorter lifespans could lead to increased replacement cycles.

The costs for building AI-optimized data centers have significantly risen, with estimates suggesting $15 million to $20 million per megawatt compared to earlier cloud facilities that averaged around $10 million per megawatt. In addition, the evolving nature of chip architecture, with the potential for a shift from GPUs to more cost-effective ASICs, further complicates investment calculations, determined by whether the demand for compute is elastic or inelastic.

Lastly, the analysis identifies that various factors influencing the AI ecosystem—such as the training versus inference workload balance, without adjusting the baseline capital estimates significantly—primarily affect timing rather than the magnitude of total investment. Bottlenecks in deployment are highlighted as risks that could affect investor confidence, although they do not necessarily change the amount of infrastructure required.

The report concludes by stressing that the capital needed for the AI build-out isn't static; rather, it fluctuates based on evolving assumptions regarding technology and market dynamics, highlighting the importance for investors and operators to continuously reassess their foundational assumptions.

summaries.title: Pennsylvania Supreme Court Reinforces the Finality of the Construction Statute of Repose
summaries.summaryText:
A May report from Clark Hill discusses the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's decision in Clearfield County v. Transystems, et al., issued on April 30, which reinforces the finality of the construction statute of repose. The court's majority opinion outlined that the case involved whether Clearfield County could use the doctrine of nullus tempus to escape the 12-year construction statute of repose established in Section 5536 of the Judicial Code. 

The Supreme Court upheld the lower courts' decisions that dismissed Clearfield County's complaint against construction professionals regarding alleged defects in a jail roof designed and built around 1977. Clearfield County argued that public entities should be exempt from this statute based on nullus tempus, which translates to "no time runs against the king." However, the Supreme Court found that nullum tempus is a tolling doctrine and is incompatible with the statute of repose, which is not subject to tolling.

The judgment emphasizes the legislature's aim to serve public interest by limiting the liability of construction professionals to a 12-year period after project completion, regardless of any circumstances preventing timely legal action. Additionally, the article references a prior piece by Clark Hill concerning the construction statute of repose and notes ongoing litigation in Aloia v. Diament, where plaintiffs are claiming violations of building codes that may toll the statute. The ruling in Clearfield County clarifies the application of the construction statute of repose, enabling construction professionals to confidently defend against claims that fall outside the specified period.

Source URL: https://www.clarkhill.com/news-events/news/pennsylvania-supreme-court-reinforces-the-finality-of-the-construction-statute-of-repose/

He highlighted that 42% of larger contractors are involved in data center projects, compared to only 7% of smaller contractors. The backlog for those working on data centers averages 12.2 months, whereas it is 8.3 months for those not engaged in such projects.

Despite the disparity in backlog size, contractors across all sizes maintain a positive outlook, with only 1 in 5 anticipating a decrease in profit margins over the next six months— the lowest since January 2025. They remain optimistic about sales and staffing levels as well, with external factors like decreased construction spending, rising oil prices, and increasing material costs not dampening member confidence.

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/abc-contractor-backlog-and-confidence-rise-again-in-april-buoyed-by-data-centers

The report highlights that the latest Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) indicates that commercial real estate (CRE) lending standards remain unchanged but show a divergence between large and small banks, especially in construction lending. 

The upcoming Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Producer Price Index (PPI) data, expected on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively, will be critical in assessing whether inflation pressures are broadening beyond energy sectors. Previous data showed a significant gap between headline and core CPI, mainly attributable to energy costs. The implications for CRE involve interest rates and refinancing considerations, along with signals for construction costs and operating expenses derived from PPI.

On Friday, the report anticipates the release of April's Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization statistics, which will shed light on potential stabilization in industrial activity following a March decline. These data points are relevant for CRE, as they can influence space demand and the credit environment for production-related borrowers.

Additionally, the May Empire State Manufacturing Survey, due on Friday, will provide early insights into manufacturing conditions, prices, and investment intentions. The previous month noted an improvement in activity alongside a softening in capital spending plans. The survey's insights on cost pressures and investment intentions will be significant for understanding manufacturing's impact on CRE.

Overall, these economic releases will inform on the breadth of inflationary pressures, the stabilization of manufacturing activity, and the influence of cost pressures on investment plans, all during a transition in Federal Reserve leadership.

summaries.title: ABC: Nonresidential Construction Adds Healthy 19,000 Jobs in April
summaries.summaryText:
A May 8 report from the Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) details the employment changes in the construction sector for April. According to an analysis of data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the construction industry saw a net increase of 9,000 jobs in April. Year-over-year, employment in the industry has grown by 50,000 jobs, marking a 0.6% increase.

Focusing specifically on nonresidential construction, the sector experienced a substantial gain of 19,000 jobs, with increases across all subcategories. The nonresidential specialty trade led the growth, contributing 12,600 new positions. In addition, nonresidential building and heavy and civil engineering jobs increased by 5,600 and 800, respectively.

In terms of unemployment, the construction sector reported a rate of 3.8% in April. This remained steady, while the overall unemployment rate for all industries was unchanged at 4.3%, which is 0.1 percentage point higher compared to the previous year.

Anirban Basu, ABC Chief Economist, noted, “Construction employment expanded modestly in April, but that’s largely due to weakness on the residential side of the industry.” He highlighted that nonresidential construction employment showed a robust increase, rising 2.0% over the past year. Basu attributed this growth to a significant rise in data center construction spending, which has surged by 34% over the past year. He also indicated that ABC member expectations for hiring remain optimistic, as shown by the Construction Confidence Index, despite slower overall job growth in the industry.

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/abc-nonresidential-construction-adds-healthy-19000-jobs-in-april

summaries.title: Dodge Momentum Index Accelerates 6% in April
summaries.summaryText:
A May 7 report from Dodge Construction Network reveals that the Dodge Momentum Index (DMI) increased by 6.2% in April, reaching 264.2, up from a revised March reading of 248.8. This growth was driven by an 8.1% rise in commercial planning and a 1.5% improvement in institutional planning. Sarah Martin, Director of Economic Research at Dodge Construction Network, noted, “After three months of slowing momentum, nonresidential planning began to find its footing in April.” However, she cautioned that macroeconomic challenges persist, including labor shortages and supply chain disruptions.

In April, planning activity increased for traditional office buildings, data centers, warehouses, hotels, and parking garages, while retail store planning experienced a slowdown. Within the institutional sector, education and healthcare project planning saw a resurgence, although recreational, public, and religious planning activity declined. Compared to April 2025, the DMI increased by 14.1%, with the commercial segment up 37.2% (5.8% without data centers) and institutional projects up 28.8%.

Throughout March, 44 planning projects valued at $100 million or more were initiated, including major developments like the $500 million Google Data Center in West Virginia and several large institutional projects such as the $256 million Navy Seal Museum in California. The DMI is an important monthly indicator reflecting the planning activity for nonresidential building projects, which typically predicts construction spending in this sector up to 18 months in advance. 

Source URL: https://www.construction.com/dodge-momentum-index/dodge-momentum-index-accelerates-6-in-april/

With significant increases in sectors like traditional office buildings, data centers, and education projects, experts suggest this uptick could foreshadow a wave of renewed construction activity. However, challenges such as labor shortages and supply chain issues continue to loom large on the horizon.

summaries.title: ABC: Construction Materials Prices Soar in April, Up 6.2% Since January
summaries.summaryText:
A May report from the Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) reveals significant increases in construction materials prices. Construction input prices rose by 1.7% in April compared to March, with nonresidential construction prices climbing by 1.8%. Year-over-year, overall construction input prices are up 7.0%, while nonresidential input prices increased by 7.4%. The report highlights substantial increases in all three energy subcategories, with crude petroleum prices soaring by 11.3% in April. Unprocessed energy materials and natural gas prices also saw increases of 9.2% and 4.9%, respectively.

ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu emphasized the rapid rise in input prices, stating, “Construction input prices surged again in April.” He noted that the 6.2% increase in the first four months of 2026 has surpassed the total rise of 4.8% over the previous three years. Basu attributed much of this escalation to soaring oil prices, but highlighted that the increase was widespread, particularly affecting tariff-impacted materials such as iron and steel.

Basu added context regarding the broader economic environment, saying, “In addition to the direct impact of this reemerging materials price escalation, too-hot inflation data coupled with upbeat labor market indicators suggest that the Federal Reserve is unlikely to cut rates this year.” He concluded by noting that while contractors remain busy, as indicated by ABC’s Construction Backlog Indicator, the ongoing cost pressures could influence construction activity in the forthcoming months.

Source URL: https://www.abc.org/News-Media/News-Releases/abc-construction-materials-prices-soar-in-april-up-62-since-january

summaries.title: Surging Materials And Energy Costs Drive Construction Input Prices Sharply Higher In April, Forcing Contractors To Pay More For Key Supplies
summaries.summaryText:
A May report from AGC Construction Data details that the producer price index for inputs to new nonresidential construction increased by 1.7 percent in April and 6.6 percent compared to April 2025. The producer price index specifically for new nonresidential building construction rose only 3.6 percent over the same period. Association officials commented that proposals to suspend the federal gas tax would not effectively mitigate these rising costs. Macrina Wilkins, director of market insights for the Associated General Contractors of America, stated, “Construction input costs continue to rise much faster than contractors’ bid prices, particularly for energy-intensive and metals-related materials,” highlighting difficulties in pricing projects amidst cost volatility, which could lead to delays and redesigns. 

Source URL: https://news.agc.org/economics/surging-materials-and-energy-costs-drive-construction-input-prices-sharply-higher-in-april-forcing-contractors-to-pay-more-for-key-supplies/
